value.overview: The Gray-throated Leaftosser (Sclerurus albigularis) is a secretive, ground-dwelling songbird of the ovenbird family. It is named for its habit of tossing aside dead leaves while searching for small prey. The species has a mainly brown and rufous plumage, a contrasting pale grayish throat, and a broad dark tail. It is usually detected by movement in leaf litter or by its sharp, distinctive calls rather than by prolonged views.
value.classification: The Gray-throated Leaftosser belongs to the order Passeriformes and the ovenbird family Furnariidae. It is one of the leaftossers, a small group of forest birds specialized for feeding in leaf litter.
value.identification: This medium-sized leaftosser is about 18 cm long. Its upperparts are generally warm rufous-brown, while the breast is darker and more reddish, creating a strong contrast with the whitish to grayish throat. The tail is broad, rounded, and dark. It has a sturdy, slightly curved bill and subdued earth-toned plumage suited to the forest floor. In Costa Rica, careful attention is needed to separate it from other brown forest-floor birds and leaftossers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species has a disjunct range from Costa Rica and western Panama through northern and western South America, including parts of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, and Trinidad and Tobago. In Costa Rica, the resident subspecies Sclerurus albigularis canigularis occurs locally in humid evergreen forest on both slopes, especially in foothill and lower montane areas, generally from about 600 m upward. It is absent or scarce in the dry northwest and favors mature forest with deep leaf litter.
value.migrationStatus: Gray-throated Leaftossers are year-round residents. In Costa Rica, the species is not considered a regular migrant; individuals remain in suitable forest habitat throughout the year, although local movements may occur when conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding information is limited, particularly for Costa Rica. Elsewhere, nesting has been reported in natural cavities, banks, or similar sheltered sites near the ground, where the bird lays eggs and raises its young away from the open forest floor. The species' breeding season is documented from October to May in Trinidad, while records from Colombia include at least May and June. The exact nesting period and nest details in Costa Rica remain poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Gray-throated Leaftosser feeds mainly on small invertebrates and other prey found in leaf litter and surface soil. Recorded food includes beetles, spiders, cockroaches, and tiny frogs. It usually forages alone or in pairs, hopping across the ground while flipping leaves aside with its bill, probing beneath them, and gleaning exposed prey. It generally does not participate in mixed-species foraging flocks.
value.behavior: This is a shy and inconspicuous forest-floor bird that usually stays under dense vegetation and is easy to overlook. It moves by hopping rather than walking and often pauses while searching beneath leaves. It is normally solitary or found in pairs. Its repeated leaf-tossing movements are characteristic, but the bird may freeze or retreat quickly when disturbed. Vocal activity can help reveal its presence in thick forest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified, but the species is considered widespread and not currently facing a level of decline that meets a threatened-category threshold.
